title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
hook: a lamp set on the doorstep lights the room and the street at once, and Tulsidas says the tongue is that doorstep
carry: a lamp on the doorstep of the tongue

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: om namah shivaya, a line from a hymn that bows to the potter and the carpenter, a bow to everyone. Who got your silent bow? Day nine hundred eighty-nine.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA, A BOW TO EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: One small clay lamp, and evening coming on. Put it inside, and the house is lit but the path outside is dark. Put it out in the lane, and the house goes black. Or set it right on the threshold, the step of the open door, where its light falls both ways at once. Tulsidas, the poet who retold the Ramayana in the language of ordinary people, takes that small household choice and turns it into a teaching about a name. Today's song is that name, Rama's.
screen: `ONE LAMP, ONE CHOICE.` → `INSIDE, OUTSIDE, OR THE DOORSTEP.` → `TODAY'S SONG: RAMA'S NAME.`

segments.voice: Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram. Honor to Rama, victory to Rama, victory, victory to Rama. At a kirtan it goes back and forth like a rocking boat. Some groups sing it for a long time without changing a word. Why would anyone want only the name, over and over? Near the start of the Ramcharitmanas, Tulsidas stops the story before it begins and spends a long stretch praising Rama's name. In one couplet he gives the lamp picture. In paraphrase: set the jewel-lamp of Rama's name on the threshold of your tongue, if you want light both inside and outside. The tongue is the doorway between the self and the world. A name kept there lights both. Inside, the mind steadies. Outside, the words that leave your mouth come out a little different. Then Tulsidas pushes further, and this is the part that can startle. He argues that, in a way, the name is greater than Rama himself. Rama, in the story, came in person and helped those he met. The name, Tulsidas says, has gone on helping countless people who never met him at all. A king can only be in one kingdom. A name can be on every doorstep. Ideas like this stand behind nama-kirtan, the singing of the name. In Tulsidas's picture, the name needs only a tongue to rest on, and anyone can say it, anywhere. That's why the song is so plain. The plainness is the point.
screen: `SHRI RAM, JAI RAM, JAI JAI RAM.` · `A LAMP ON THE TONGUE'S DOORSTEP.` · `LIGHT INSIDE AND OUTSIDE.` · `THE NAME REACHES WHERE RAMA DIDN'T.` · then, large: `THE PLAINNESS IS THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Let the mouth relax, lips just touching. Rest your attention on the tongue, lying quiet behind the teeth. That's the doorstep. If you pray, you can set Rama's name there, saying it silently: Ram. Ram. Let it sit in the doorway and see whether it lights anything, inside or out. If you'd rather not use the name, rest your attention on that doorway anyway, and notice what wants to come out of it today. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram, Rama's name set like a lamp on the doorstep of the tongue.
Your line: a lamp on the doorstep of the tongue. Today, before one hard conversation, pause at the doorstep of your tongue and choose what you set there. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: At kirtan, Shri Ram jai Ram jai jai Ram is sung back and forth, sometimes for a long stretch without changing a word; some Hindus also repeat Rama's name quietly through the day.

fork.setup: you have one clay lamp at nightfall. you want light in the house and on the path. where do you put it?
options: on the threshold of the open door.
fork.reveal: on the threshold, its light falls both ways. Tulsidas says to set Rama's name there, on the doorstep of the tongue.

original.note: Rama's name, written in Devanagari. In nama-kirtan, the name alone is the song.

trapdoor: what you thought: chanting Ram is just repeating a name.
what it means: for Tulsidas the name is a lamp on the tongue's doorstep, lighting inside and outside at once.
what a scholar hears: before his story begins, Tulsidas spends a long stretch on the name, and argues it is in some ways greater than Rama himself.

notes: Index title/word/carry kept exactly; spoken carry reads '(20 songs)' as 'twenty songs'.
Doha 21 (rama nama manidipa dharu jiha dehari dvara...) paraphrased as the jewel-lamp on the threshold of the tongue; confirm number and gloss.
The name-greater-than-Rama argument is summarized loosely from the nama-mahima section (e.g. Rama saved one, the name saves countless); confirm the paraphrase and the doha range.
'Before electric light, a family with one small clay lamp' is an illustrative scene, not a historical claim.
'Tulsidas, the poet who retold the Ramayana in the language of ordinary people' (Awadhi); confirm wording.
'Shri Ram jai Ram jai jai Ram': no attribution is given for the chant; some associate it with Samarth Ramdas. Left out on purpose.

Editor pass: hook no longer makes a historical claim about households 'before electric light'; the narrator's 'it doesn't ask for learning, money or a temple' (not in the cited dohas) replaced with Tulsidas's own picture; the first myth item rewritten so its answer comes from the script.
Audit: hook said Tulsidas's doha teaches 'about a song'; it is about the name, now says so. Cut a repeated 'anyone who says it, anywhere'. Practice opener changed from stock 'sit comfortably'.
